items.title: Why the server sets the settings discriminator
items.body:
For each post, `mapTypeToPost` loads the integration with `getIntegrationById(organization, post.integration.id)` and returns `settings: { ...(post.settings || {}), __type: integration.providerIdentifier }`. The client's settings are spread first, so the `__type` written after them wins. The discriminator in `CreatePostDto` then chooses the settings class of the real provider, so a client cannot pick a looser DTO.

- *The client's 'x'*: it is overwritten before validation runs.
- *A 400 on mismatch*: the code never compares the two values.
- *Both, keeping whichever passes*: only one discriminator value exists after the spread.

items.title: Why saving as a draft stops the post workflow
items.body:
`startWorkflow` always begins by listing running workflows with this `postId` and terminating each one that is not already terminated. Only then does it check the state: `if (state === 'DRAFT') return;`. So a post moved back to draft ends up with no running workflow, and nothing will publish it until it is scheduled again, which starts a fresh `post_<id>` workflow.

- *A new workflow that sleeps*: the early return skips `workflow.start`.
- *The old workflow keeps going*: it was just terminated.
- *A poke signal*: that is the missing-post sweep's `signalWithStart`, a different path.

items.title: Why draft settings are not validated
items.body:
In `create.post.dto.ts` the `settings` property is decorated with `@ValidateIf((o) => o.type !== 'draft')` above `@ValidateNested()`. In class-validator, when a `ValidateIf` condition is false, all other validators on that property are ignored. For a draft, the incomplete settings pass, and problems appear only when the draft is later scheduled and validated again.

- *Nested DTOs are always checked*: ValidateIf exists to switch them off.
- *A default value fills the gap*: nothing supplies defaults here.
- *Converted to a schedule*: only `replaceDraft` in `mapTypeToPost` changes the type, and it is false on this path.

items.title: Start here: Postiz, a social scheduler built on NestJS and Temporal
items.body:
This repository (named gitroom here) is a checkout of Postiz, an open-source tool that schedules posts to 30+ social networks. The code lives under `postiz-app/`: `apps/backend` is the NestJS API, `apps/orchestrator` runs Temporal workflows and activities, and `libraries/nestjs-libraries` holds the services and Prisma repositories both processes share. The study course is `postiz-app/fabledocs/upskill/`.

Read, in order:

1. `03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`.
2. `03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md`.
3. `03-architecture-and-patterns/06-architecture-critique.md`.
4. `09-reference/risk-register.md`.

The guides mark each claim as *Confirmed* or *Investigate*. Every link points at a line range; open it and check the claim yourself, because the quiz asks what the code does. If a word like Temporal, workflow or activity is new, read `01-codebase-cartography/01-system-map.md` first.

items.title: Why the Postiz JWT never expires
items.body:
`signJWT(value)` is `sign(value, process.env.JWT_SECRET!)`, with no options object. jsonwebtoken adds an `exp` claim only when you pass `expiresIn` (or set `exp` yourself), so these tokens have no expiry. The value signed is the user object handed in, so the token carries the whole row, and a role change is not reflected until a new token is issued.

- *Seven days from JWT_EXPIRES*: no such option is read here.
- *Until logout with a denylist*: verifyJWT only checks the signature; no denylist is consulted.
- *One hour by default*: jsonwebtoken has no default lifetime.

items.title: Why a handler with no policies passes the guard
items.body:
`canActivate` first returns `true` for a few path substrings. It then reads the `CHECK_POLICIES_KEY` metadata with `|| []` and, if the list is empty, returns `true`. Plan limits are evaluated only for handlers that declare `@CheckPolicies`. The guard is a capability gate, not a default-deny boundary.

- *Denied by default*: the code returns true for an empty list.
- *Self-hosted only*: the self-hosted check sits in `PermissionsService`, which is never called here.
- *Throws for missing metadata*: there is no throw on this path.

items.title: Concept: Temporal workflows, activities and their side effects
items.body:
Temporal runs **workflows**: durable functions whose state survives restarts. A workflow may only do deterministic work; anything that touches the outside world runs in an **activity**, which Temporal can retry according to a retry policy. A workflow has an id, and a conflict policy decides what happens when you start a workflow whose id is already running.

In Postiz, each scheduled post gets its own workflow. Read:

- `proxyTaskQueue` at the top of `apps/orchestrator/src/workflows/post-workflows/post.workflow.v1.0.5.ts`. Look up what `maximumAttempts`, `initialInterval` and `backoffCoefficient` mean in the Temporal docs, then compute the schedule this policy gives.
- `startWorkflow` in `posts.service.ts`. List its steps in order, including any early return, and note the workflow id and conflict policy it uses.
- `createPost` in the same file: how is `startWorkflow` called, and what happens to its errors?
- `sendWebhooks` in `apps/orchestrator/src/activities/post.activity.ts`: follow one delivery and its error handling.
- `libraries/nestjs-libraries/src/temporal/infinite.workflow.register.ts`: when does the missing-post sweep start?

Then grade each side effect yourself before you read the guide's table.

items.title: Why an unlisted controller is unauthenticated
items.body:
`ApiModule.configure()` runs `consumer.apply(AuthMiddleware).forRoutes(...authenticatedController)`. The middleware is attached only to controllers in that array. A controller registered in `controllers` but not in the list is still served, just without the middleware that verifies the JWT and loads the user and organization. The guide calls this fail-open: forgetting one line ships an unauthenticated endpoint.

- *Nest refuses to boot*: middleware is optional; Nest boots fine.
- *Applied to the whole module*: `forRoutes` limits it to the listed controllers.
- *401 by default*: nothing produces a 401 when no middleware runs.

items.title: Why a failing activity runs three times, 2 minutes apart
items.body:
In Temporal, `maximumAttempts` counts every attempt, including the first, so 3 means one try plus two retries. The wait before the first retry is `initialInterval` (2 minutes), and each later wait is the previous one times `backoffCoefficient`. With a coefficient of 1 the wait stays at 2 minutes.

- *Doubling waits*: that would need a coefficient of 2.
- *Five attempts every 5 seconds*: those numbers belong to other retry layers (the provider fetch and the refresh loop), not to this policy.
- *Unlimited until 10 minutes*: `startToCloseTimeout` limits one attempt; `maximumAttempts` caps the series.

items.title: Why an unreachable webhook fails silently
items.body:
`sendWebhooks` maps every matching webhook to an async function whose body is `try { await fetch(webhook.url, {...}) } catch (e) { /**empty**/ }`, and awaits them with `Promise.all`. A network error is caught and dropped, so every promise resolves and the activity completes as a success. With no failure there is nothing for Temporal to retry, and no record is written. The guide grades outgoing webhooks D: unsigned, no retry, no delivery log.

- *Temporal retries it*: the activity never throws.
- *A failed delivery row*: there is no delivery log table.
- *Signed and retried with backoff*: there is neither a signature nor a retry.

items.title: Why setNickname is safe despite an id-only write
items.body:
Before anything is written, `setNickname` calls `getIntegrationById(org.id, id)`, which looks the integration up within the caller's organization, and throws `Invalid integration` if nothing comes back. So a foreign id stops there, and the id-only `updateNameAndUrl` is reached only for the caller's own integration. The risk register notes that the guard lives in the caller, not in the query, which is fragile if another caller reuses the update.

- *A rolling-back transaction*: there is no transaction in this method.
- *AuthMiddleware checks ids*: the middleware resolves the user and organization; it does not inspect path ids.
- *orgId inside updateNameAndUrl*: the update is keyed by id alone, which is why the earlier check matters.

items.title: Why editTag can rename another organization tag
items.body:
The controller passes `org.id` down, and `editTag(id, orgId, body)` receives it, but its Prisma call is `update({ where: { id }, data: {...} })`. The organization is never part of the filter, so any existing tag id is updated, whoever owns it. That is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference). `deleteTag`, the next method, shows the fix: `where: { id, orgId }`.

- *Not-found error*: that is what would happen if orgId were in the where, as in deleteTag.
- *A copy in organization A*: the call is an update, not a create.
- *PoliciesGuard refuses it*: the guard checks plan and role policies; it knows nothing about who owns a tag.

items.title: Why the any body is validated in the service
items.body:
Nest's `ValidationPipe` validates a parameter against its declared class. A parameter typed `any` gives it no class to validate, so the global pipe passes `rawBody` through unchanged. `mapTypeToPost` makes up for it: after mapping each post, it builds `new ValidationPipe({ skipMissingProperties: false, transform: true, ... })` and calls `transform(mappedValues, { type: 'body', metatype: CreatePostDto })`.

- *The global pipe reads the service's DTO*: pipes see only the parameter's own type.
- *Unvalidated*: the service-level pipe does validate it.
- *PoliciesGuard validates the body*: guards run before pipes and only check policies.

excerpts.quote: return await validationPipe.transform(mappedValues, { type: 'body', metatype: CreatePostDto, });

items.title: Concept: identity, plan gates and ownership are three layers
items.body:
The validation guide splits security into validation, authentication and authorization, and splits authorization again into plan/role gates and resource ownership. Trace each layer in code.

- **Authentication.** In `apps/backend/src/api/api.module.ts`, find `authenticatedController` and the `configure()` method. Work out which controllers `AuthMiddleware` is applied to. Then open `libraries/helpers/src/auth/auth.service.ts` and read `signJWT`: note every argument passed to `sign`.
- **Plan gates.** Read `canActivate` in `apps/backend/src/services/auth/permissions/permissions.guard.ts` top to bottom and list each early `return`.
- **Ownership.** Run the guide's IDOR audit on `posts.repository.ts`: for each `update` or `delete`, check whether the organization id is in the `where`. Then look at `setNickname` in `integrations.controller.ts` and note what runs before its write.
- **Validation.** Compare how `@Body()` is typed in `createPost` (`posts.controller.ts`) with the global pipe in `main.ts`, then read `mapTypeToPost` in `posts.service.ts`, including how it builds `settings`. Finally read the decorators on `settings` in `create.post.dto.ts` and the file pipe in `upload/custom.upload.validation.ts`.

items.title: Why a renamed PDF is rejected
items.body:
`CustomFileValidationPipe` calls `fromBuffer(value.buffer)` (the file-type library), which reads the file's leading magic bytes. It then checks the detected mime against `ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES`. The file name and the client-sent `mimetype` play no part. A PDF is detected as `application/pdf`, which is not on the list, so the pipe throws `BadRequestException('Unsupported file type.')` before the size check.

- *Accepted for image/png*: the client mimetype is never consulted.
- *Renamed and stored*: the pipe only validates; it never rewrites files.
- *Accepted under a size limit*: the type check fails first, and size is checked only for allowed types.
